incidents.name: Na Lao irrigation weir
incidents.cause_summary: Heavy rain and strong currents washed away one side of the Na Lao irrigation weir and damaged the adjacent road.
incidents.what_happened: Heavy rain across Nan Province on 19 August 2026 damaged irrigation and road infrastructure. Khaosod English, citing the Nan provincial public relations office, reported that strong currents washed away one side of the Na Lao irrigation weir in Santi Suk district and damaged the road beside it. The same storm cut the Phayaeng–Kiew Muang approach to the provincial capital, stranded people on a Muap-stream bridge at Ban Nam Song, and was reported with a Highway 1256 (Pua–Bo Kluea) bridge collapse. Nation Thailand separately described flash floods and washed-out bridges in Pua, including a bridge in the Fai Chao weir area — a different named structure. No source fetched reported deaths at the Na Lao weir itself.

NSEMA Director-General Abdullahi Baba Arah said August rains raised the need for immediate technical assessment and that a major failure could flood downstream communities in Kaduna, Niger State, the FCT and adjoining areas. NSEMA asked the federal government, Kaduna State, dam operators, NEMA, the hydrological and meteorological agencies and security services to verify crack severity, map downstream risk and activate early warning and evacuation planning. Residents were told to stay calm, avoid waterways in heavy rain and ignore unverified rumours. No source fetched for this dataset reported a breach or uncontrolled release.
incidents.status: No breach reported as of 19 August 2026. Neighbouring-state emergency agency alert only; independent confirmation of crack severity by Kaduna/NEMA/dam operator not found in the articles fetched.

incidents.name: Lake Wynonah Dam
incidents.region: South Manheim Township, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania
incidents.location_label: South Manheim Township, Pennsylvania, United States
incidents.cause_summary: This is a watch, not a confirmed failure: PADEP cited severe internal erosion, a crumbling concrete spillway and inability to pass a major flood.
incidents.what_happened: In a 14 August 2026 letter to the Lake Wynonah Property Owners Association, Kirk Kreider, acting chief of PADEP's Division of Dam Safety, declared the 1971 earthen Lake Wynonah Dam 'unsafe' and requested an immediate voluntary full drawdown of the 175-acre reservoir at up to one foot per day, with a formal order threatened if the association does not comply. The letter cited severe internal erosion, a crumbling concrete spillway, inability to pass a major flood, and temporary bracing of the top walls after a spillway collapse at the community's Fawn Lake Dam. Kreider wrote that 'unsafe' does not mean imminent failure, but that deficiencies could result in failure with loss of life or substantial property damage if not corrected. The lake had already been drawn down 10–15 feet in autumn 2025 after new seepage and a boil were reported. PADEP also said the high-hazard owner lacked required financial assurance.
incidents.status: PADEP unsafe designation and requested full drawdown in effect as of 17 August 2026 reporting; draft consent order/agreement with a four-week response window. Not an imminent-failure declaration.
incidents.notes: 2025 seepage drawdown is background. No 2026 breach. Fawn Lake Dam spillway collapse date was not independently sourced for this file.

incidents.river_or_facility: Kansas River (Kaw) / Bowersock Mills & Power Company
incidents.cause_summary: Owner said one of four inflatable rubber crest bladders was punctured by floating trees and debris and ripped from end to end; the concrete dam remained intact.
incidents.what_happened: The Lawrence Journal-World reported on 13 August 2026 that one of four inflatable rubber bladders on the crest of Bowersock Dam had been punctured by heavy floating debris and ripped from end to end. Co-owner Sarah Hill-Nelson said the No. 2 bladder failure left a gap that dropped the upstream millpond about six feet. The concrete dam was holding; there was no downstream flood wave. The city of Lawrence said the Kaw River Water Treatment Plant continued to operate, though low pond levels are less efficient for intake and filtration. The run-of-river dam supplies Kansas's only hydroelectric plant and maintains the pond for the city's water intake. Hill-Nelson said a replacement bladder would take about four months and cost upwards of $300,000, and that this was the first time a Lawrence bladder had been destroyed beyond repair (a 2021 seam tear had been stitched). Exact calendar day of the puncture was described only as recently before the Thursday 13 August article.

incidents.name: Beiru River and Jialu River levee breaches
incidents.region: Henan (Jiaxian County, Pingdingshan; Chuanhui District, Zhoukou)
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia (Changqiao Town, Jiaxian); Xinhua: Yuxi Village Beiru breach
incidents.cause_summary: Heavy rain from remnants of Typhoon Dolphin opened levee breaches on the Beiru and Jialu rivers.
incidents.what_happened: Heavy rain from remnants of Typhoon Dolphin opened a levee breach more than 40 metres wide on the Beiru River in Jiaxian County, Pingdingshan, on the night of Wednesday 12 August 2026; more than 2,000 people were relocated and Xinhua reported no casualties. That breach was sealed on Friday night 14 August after nearly two days of sandbagging, because heavy plant could not reach the narrow levee crown. A separate eastern-embankment breach on the Jialu River in Chuanhui District, Zhoukou, opened around 23:00 on Thursday 13 August, widening from about 30 metres to about 117 metres under Jialu inflows and Shaying River backwater. China Daily and People's Daily/Xinhua said the Jialu breach was sealed on Saturday night 15 August after more than 2,000 emergency personnel worked the site; crews continued raising, reinforcing and sealing seepage. A Level-IV national disaster-relief response was activated for Henan.
incidents.status: Both breaches reported sealed (Beiru 14 Aug; Jialu 15 Aug). Embankment raising, reinforcement and seepage control continuing at Jialu as of 15–16 August 2026.
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: More than 2,000 relocated from the Beiru breach; Jialu displacement not separately quantified in the English Xinhua/China Daily reports used
incidents.notes: Two distinct levee breaches grouped as one living-database item because they were the same Typhoon Dolphin flood episode. Zero deaths is the Beiru figure stated by Xinhua; no separate Jialu fatality figure was published in the reports fetched.

incidents.cause_summary: Intense rain was followed by failure of the primary spillway pipe; DCR said it had received none of the required owner documents since 2006 and the last emergency action plan expired in 2012.
incidents.what_happened: Intense rain on the night of 2 August 2026 flooded the Laurel Fork area of Carroll County. Virginia DCR Regional Engineer Steven Bricker observed on 4 August that the Olde Mill Golf Club lake (normal pool near 300 acre-feet) was almost completely drained after a partial breach. Owners were dewatering and beginning repairs as of mid-August; Carroll County said it issued no live alert because it learned of the flood after it ended.

incidents.name: Cement Lake Dam (Portland Reservoir)
incidents.location_label: West El Paso, Texas, United States
incidents.river_or_facility: Cement Lake / Portland Reservoir (spring-fed; pump-down toward Rio Grande culverts)
incidents.cause_summary: This is a watch, not a confirmed failure: engineers saw slow slope failures, embankment movement and seepage consistent with a possible breach before the dam was stabilised.
incidents.what_happened: El Paso Water, which acquired Cement Lake and about 300 acres from TxDOT in late March 2026, issued urgent updates on 23 April 2026 after engineers saw slow slope failures, slight embankment movement and seepage — indicators it said were consistent with a possible breach. Personnel were pulled to higher ground; USACE advisers were brought in; pumping began and roads including approaches toward Doniphan and Paisano were closed. EPWater said nearby homes sit on higher ground and were not expected to flood. incidents.cause_summary: Hand-built earth/peat/stone dam sealed in winter failed under spring-flood pressure on first filling/operation; eastern canal was incorrectly graded.
incidents.what_happened: On the opening day of a 1929–1932 timber-floating reservoir, the eastern canal/sluice released little water because it had been dug too shallow. The eastern gate was closed so the canal could be improved; around 19:00 the poorly built western dam failed during spring flood. incidents.name: Schaeffer Dam (Lake McNeil / Beaver Creek Dam)
incidents.location_label: Beaver Creek above Penrose, Fremont County, Colorado, United States

incidents.name: Mammoth Dam (Gooseberry Creek)
incidents.location_label: Gooseberry Creek, about 80 miles southeast of Salt Lake City, Utah, United States

incidents.name: Walnut Grove Dam
incidents.location_label: Hassayampa River north of Wickenburg, Arizona, United States
incidents.cause_summary: A rockfill dam with an undersized spillway (final roughly 26 by 7 ft, about 2,200 cfs) was overtopped by an estimated 25-year flood after days of rain. Construction had been repeatedly cheapened; a messenger sent to warn downstream camps got drunk and never delivered the warning.
incidents.what_happened: After about 7 inches of rain from 16 February 1890, Walnut Grove Dam on the Hassayampa River overtopped about 21:00 on 21 February and failed shortly after midnight on 22 February. About 4 billion gallons rushed down the canyon, destroying the diversion-dam workers' camp and settlements toward Wickenburg. Commonly cited deaths exceed 100; some accounts put the toll as high as 150. The dam was never rebuilt.
incidents.status: historical / not rebuilt; remnants of spillway and diversion tunnel remain
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: workers' camp and downstream Hassayampa settlements destroyed
incidents.notes: Commonly cited figure is 100+; Dill and later summaries say as many as 150. Early New York Times headline said 40. Use 100 and record the range here.
incidents.volume_released: about 4 billion US gallons (15 billion litres)

incidents.name: South Fork Dam (Johnstown Flood)
incidents.river_or_facility: South Fork Little Conemaugh River / Lake Conemaugh
incidents.cause_summary: After days of heavy rain the earthfill dam overtopped and failed, after modifications that lowered the crest, clogged the spillway with fish screens and removed discharge pipes.
incidents.what_happened: After days of heavy rain, the earthfill South Fork Dam owned by the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club overtopped and failed at about 15:15, releasing Lake Conemaugh toward Johnstown. Modifications that lowered the crest, clogged the spillway with fish screens and removed discharge pipes reduced freeboard and outlet capacity. The debris-laden wave destroyed towns along the Little Conemaugh and burned at the Stone Bridge in Johnstown.
incidents.status: historical / Johnstown Flood National Memorial at the dam site
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: 1,600 homes lost; Johnstown and upstream valley towns destroyed

incidents.owner_operator: South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club

incidents.volume_released: Lake Conemaugh (about 20 million tons of water)
incidents.downstream_risk: Johnstown and towns along the Little Conemaugh

incidents.name: Williamsburg Reservoir Dam (Mill River Flood)
incidents.geo_source: OpenStreetMap Historic Dam Trail terminus (dam ruins)
incidents.cause_summary: A poorly constructed earthen reservoir dam failed; the Hampshire County coroner's jury found fault with the reservoir company, engineers, contractors and weak state regulation.
incidents.what_happened: A poorly constructed earthen reservoir dam on the Mill River above Williamsburg, Massachusetts, failed and sent a flood wave through Williamsburg, Skinnerville, Haydenville and Leeds. The Hampshire County coroner's jury found fault with the reservoir company, engineers, contractors and weak state regulation. It was the deadliest U.S. dam failure until Johnstown in 1889.

incidents.affected_or_evacuated: four mill villages wrecked along a narrow valley

incidents.downstream_risk: Williamsburg, Skinnerville, Haydenville and Leeds mill villages

incidents.name: Iruka Lake Dam (Irukaike / Irukagire)
incidents.location_label: Lake Iruka (Irukaike), Ikeno, Inuyama, Aichi, Japan
incidents.cause_summary: The earth irrigation dam collapsed after heavy rain from late April. Japanese disaster lists describe an embankment collapse (Irukagire) under that rainfall.
incidents.what_happened: The earthfill irrigation dam at Lake Iruka, built from the 1630s as a large agricultural reservoir, collapsed on 13 May 1868 after heavy rain from late April. Water flooded the Gojo River basin, causing severe damage in Inuyama, Iwakura, Kasugai, Tsushima, Yatomi and Komaki. Official counts record 941 deaths, 807 houses destroyed and 11,709 houses flooded. The event is known in Japan as Irukagire.
incidents.status: historical / lake still exists as a rebuilt irrigation reservoir

incidents.name: Dale Dyke Dam (Great Sheffield Flood)
incidents.cause_summary: The embankment failed during first filling; government inspectors pointed to design and construction defects in the puddle-clay core, though the exact initiating crack was never proven.
incidents.what_happened: The nearly completed earth embankment of Dale Dyke Reservoir at Bradfield failed as it was being filled for the first time, releasing roughly 3 million cubic metres of water down the Loxley valley into Sheffield. The flood destroyed mills, houses and bridges and inundated about 4,000 houses. Government inspectors later pointed to design and construction defects in the puddle-clay core, though the exact initiating crack was never proven.
incidents.status: historical / dam later rebuilt (1875); remains a landmark Victorian civil-engineering disaster
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: thousands of households flooded; 600+ houses damaged or destroyed
incidents.notes: Chief Constable recorded 240 deaths; later local research suggests additional indirect deaths not on the official list.
incidents.downstream_risk: Loxley valley and Sheffield; about 4,000 houses inundated
incidents.economic_damage: claims raised over £42,000 in contemporary relief; one of the largest Victorian insurance claims
incidents.investigating_agency: Home Office inquiry (Robert Rawlinson and Nathaniel Beardmore)

incidents.name: Bilberry Reservoir
incidents.location_label: Bilberry Reservoir, west of Holmfirth, West Yorkshire, United Kingdom
incidents.geo_source: Wikipedia Holmfirth floods coordinates (Holmfirth / Holme Valley); Bilberry dam is west of Holmfirth
incidents.cause_summary: The embankment was built over a spring that eroded the puddle-clay core so the crest slumped below the waste pit. After heavy rain the reservoir overtopped and the central embankment collapsed. The inquest found original construction defective and the Commissioners guilty of great and culpable negligence.
incidents.what_happened: About 01:00 on 5 February 1852 the Bilberry reservoir embankment west of Holmfirth collapsed, releasing about 86 million gallons down the River Holme. The flood killed 81 people and destroyed four mills, ten dye houses, 27 cottages, seven shops, seven bridges and other buildings.
incidents.status: historical / reservoir later rebuilt; 1944 Holme Valley flood was a separate thunderstorm, not a Bilberry breach
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: many left homeless and without work; four mills and 27 cottages among buildings destroyed
incidents.notes: Also called the 1852 Holmfirth Flood.

incidents.name: Hogs Back Dam (Rideau Canal)
incidents.location_label: Hogs Back (Three Rock Rapids), Rideau River, Ottawa, Canada
incidents.geo_source: Parks Canada Hogs Back lockstation GPS 45°22'12"N 75°41'56"W
incidents.cause_summary: A leak from about 28 March 1829 and slumping on 2 April led to collapse of the stone-arch dam on 3 April. Builders were inexperienced with frozen-earth versus unfrozen-core behaviour in spring flood.
incidents.what_happened: Colonel John By's stone-arch dam at Hogs Back, intended to drown the rapids between Hogs Back and Black Rapids, failed on 3 April 1829 during spring flood after earlier washouts in February and April 1828. By wrote that he felt a motion like an earthquake while standing on the leaking dam with 40 men and ordered them to run as stones fell from under his feet. The frozen crest held long enough for workers to escape. A timber-crib dam of a different design was then built on the remaining foundation the same year.
incidents.status: historical / replaced 1829 by timber-crib dam; present Hogs Back lockstation still operates

incidents.name: Puentes Dam (Puentes II)
incidents.location_label: Guadalentín River at Puentes, Lorca, Spain
incidents.geo_source: Spanish Wikipedia Embalse de Puentes (present reservoir; 1802 Puentes II stood in the same gorge)
incidents.cause_summary: The masonry dam, founded on sandy riverbed with piles, failed by piping after April rains filled the reservoir nearly to the crest. Agustín de Betancourt concluded it would not have failed if not founded on sand.
incidents.what_happened: Puentes II, a roughly 34 m masonry irrigation dam on the Guadalentín above Lorca, first filled in 1788, burst about 15:00 on 30 April 1802 after a muddy jet appeared below the dam at 14:30. The flood reached Lorca about 16:00, destroyed the San Cristóbal quarter and hundreds of houses, and continued through Totana, Alhama, Librilla and Sangonera into Murcia that night. The disaster is widely cited as a reason Spain created the Escuela de Caminos y Canales later in 1802.
incidents.status: historical / Puentes II destroyed; later dams built nearby (Puentes III 1881-84; Puentes IV 1993-2000)
incidents.affected_or_evacuated: about 600-1800 houses destroyed; huertas of Lorca and downstream towns inundated
